werk/jack-dejohnette-sorcery.text:
Jack DeJohnette recorded Sorcery in 1974, in March at Willow and in May at Bearsville Studios in New York State. The record was released on the Prestige label. Besides DeJohnette himself, who plays drums and also keyboards and saxophone, we hear Bennie Maupin on bass clarinet, the guitarists John Abercrombie and Mick Goodrick and the bassist Dave Holland. The album contains short pieces and long compositions, including Sorcery #1 and The Reverend King Suite, which consists of six parts and is partly based on music by John Coltrane.

The AllMusic reviewer called the music interesting but uneven and thought it had aged badly. At the same time he praised DeJohnette's willingness to take risks.
werk/jack-dejohnette-sorcery.listen: Listen to The Reverend King Suite and notice how the piece consists of several parts, each with a different title and mood.

werk/jaco-pastorius-holiday-for-pans.text:
Between 1980 and 1982, the bassist Jaco Pastorius recorded, in various studios in New York, the material for what was to become his third solo album, after Word of Mouth from 1981. He produced it together with Peter Yianilos. The record is above all a showcase for the steel drums of Othello Molineaux. Wayne Shorter, Don Alias and Toots Thielemans also play, and the Los Angeles Philharmonic Orchestra provides the orchestration for Mysterious Mountain.

Warner Bros. refused to release the album because it was too esoteric for a label that expected commercial fusion. It includes covers of She's Leaving Home by The Beatles and Giant Steps by John Coltrane, and the title song plays with Holiday for Strings by David Rose. Not until 1993, six years after the bassist's death, was the record released, on the Japanese label Sound Hills. The Penguin Guide to Jazz called it by far the most imaginative project he ever undertook.
werk/jaco-pastorius-holiday-for-pans.listen: Listen to the title track Holiday for Pans and notice the steel drums, which take the leading role here.

werk/jaco-pastorius-word-of-mouth.text:
Word of Mouth is the second and last solo album by the bassist Jaco Pastorius and was released in 1981, when he was still playing with Weather Report. It is also the name of the big band he put together and with which he toured in 1982. His debut mainly showcased his electric bass, but here the emphasis was more on composing and arranging for a larger group. Those playing included Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter, Peter Erskine, Jack DeJohnette, Michael Brecker and Toots Thielemans on harmonica.

Even so, the bass stands out in the solo opening of Chromatic Fantasy by Bach and in the title song. Crisis has a fast bass figure that keeps running beneath the frantic soloing. John and Mary is dedicated to his children from his first marriage. The first 50,000 copies appeared without the musicians' names, owing to a legal dispute; later they were credited. The Penguin Guide to Jazz called it a wonderful record full of surprises.
werk/jaco-pastorius-word-of-mouth.listen: Listen to Chromatic Fantasy and notice the solo opening on bass, and compare it with tracks in which the bass is more absorbed into the arrangement.

werk/james-brown-grits-en-soul.text:
Grits & Soul was James Brown's eighth album, released in August 1964 by Smash Records. He does not sing on it but plays organ, because that was how he got around his contractual obligations to King Records. On the tracks the name Ted Wright appears as composer, a pseudonym of his own.

It is an instrumental album with a line-up of musicians from Kinston, North Carolina. Nat Jones plays alto saxophone and wrote the arrangements, Melvin Parker plays drums and Robert Knight trumpet. The album also contains the first known recording of Maceo Parker, here still on baritone saxophone. In 1965 the record spent ten weeks on the Billboard chart and reached number 124.
werk/james-brown-grits-en-soul.listen: Listen to Grits and notice how the track, without any vocals, runs on organ and horns.

werk/james-horner-titanic-music-from-the.text:
Titanic: Music from the Motion Picture is the soundtrack of the film Titanic, composed, orchestrated and conducted by James Horner and performed by the Hollywood Studio Symphony. The album was released on 18 November 1997. The director James Cameron first wanted Enya to write the music. When she declined, he asked the composer, who wrote with her style in mind. The wordless vocals are by the Norwegian singer Sissel Kyrkjebø.

He wrote fixed themes for characters and events. Hymn to the Sea is a sad, wistful theme with bagpipes and voice. Southampton sounds cheerful and adventurous. The choir is digital, because he wanted to avoid a churchlike sound. My Heart Will Go On, sung by Céline Dion, he wrote with Will Jennings, without Cameron's knowledge. It won an Oscar and a Golden Globe.
werk/james-horner-titanic-music-from-the.listen: Listen to Hymn to the Sea and notice the bagpipes and the wordless voice, which together carry the wistful theme.

werk/james-newton-howard-james-newton-ho.text:
This album came about after a demonstration of the new Yamaha DX7 at the NAMM show in Anaheim in January 1983. Bill Schnee and Doug Sax of Sheffield Lab heard James Newton Howard, David Paich and Steve Porcaro play there and wanted to capture the music on record straight away. Recording was long neglected because of busy schedules. Only on 16 December, shortly before the deadline, did Sheffield get a single weekend.

The album contains almost exclusively electronic sounds. Only the drums of Jeff Porcaro, the percussion of his father Joe Porcaro and a grand piano played by Paich are acoustic. The rest comes from nine layers of Yamaha synthesizers, played live, mixed and recorded on two tracks.
werk/james-newton-howard-james-newton-ho.listen: Listen to Borealis and notice how the synthesizers sound together with the drums and percussion.

werk/james-taylor-mud-slide-slim-and-the.text:
James Taylor recorded his third studio album between early January and late February 1971. Peter Asher produced it and Warner Bros. Records released it in April of that year. Carole King played piano and Joni Mitchell sang along on a few tracks.

The best-known song is You've Got a Friend, Taylor's version of a song by Carole King. It became his only number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and earned him a Grammy. The album itself stalled at number 2, because King's own album Tapestry occupied the top spot. Long Ago and Far Away became a second hit and You Can Close Your Eyes grew into a firm favourite at his concerts. Rolling Stone at first found the record dull, but after a few listens heard a peculiar weariness that belongs to the whole.
werk/james-taylor-mud-slide-slim-and-the.listen: Listen to You've Got a Friend and notice how calmly the song is built around Taylor's voice and acoustic guitar. Can you hear that he is singing someone else's song here?

werk/james-taylor-one-man-dog.text:
One Man Dog was released on 1 November 1972 and is James Taylor's fourth studio album. Peter Asher was the producer. The basic recordings came mostly from his own home studio. The album has eighteen tracks, many of which are very short. There is also a quadraphonic mix with different vocal takes and longer versions.

At that moment he had just married Carly Simon and was off drugs. A reviewer of the time saw in the album a confirmation of that life and a turn inwards. The album reached number four in America. Don't Let Me Be Lonely Tonight reached number fourteen on the Hot 100. Critics were divided. Some praised the short tracks; AllMusic later called it a disappointment because much of it sounded sketchy and unfinished. Linda Ronstadt sings along on One Morning in May, the traditional song that one reviewer considered the best on the album.
werk/james-taylor-one-man-dog.listen: Listen to One Morning in May and notice how Taylor's voice blends with that of Linda Ronstadt.

werk/james-taylor-sweet-baby-james.text:
Sweet Baby James is James Taylor's second studio album. Producer Peter Asher recorded it in December 1969 in ten days at Sunset Sound in Los Angeles, for just 7,600 dollars. The singer was by then practically homeless and slept at Asher's or on the couch of the guitarist Danny Kortchmar. Suite for 20 G owes its name to the 20,000 dollars that had been promised to him once the album was finished. One more track was needed, so he stuck three unfinished songs together.

The sound is subdued: folk, country, gospel and blues, carefully understated. Fire and Rain reached number three on the Billboard Hot 100, Country Road number thirty-seven. The album was nominated for Album of the Year and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2002. It made Taylor one of the best-known faces of the rising singer-songwriter wave.
werk/james-taylor-sweet-baby-james.listen: In Fire and Rain, listen to how restrained the accompaniment remains and how the voice and the guitar stay in charge.

werk/jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-eart.text:
Emergency on Planet Earth is Jamiroquai's debut album and was released in June 1993. It began with When You Gonna Learn, the track with which Jay Kay made his debut on Acid Jazz Records in 1992 and which earned him a contract with Sony. When he fell out with his producer over the recording, he realised that he wanted a real live band. This is how the group around the bassist Stuart Zender, the keyboard player Toby Smith and the didgeridoo player Wallis Buchanan came into being.

The sound rests on 1970s acid jazz, funk and soul, with rich arrangements and socially engaged lyrics about, among other things, the environment and war. Too Young to Die became a British top ten hit. Kay wrote it with Smith. Revolution 1993 lasts ten minutes and Didgin' Out closes the record. The album reached number one in the United Kingdom, and Q called it a contender for the best British soul album of the 1990s.
werk/jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-eart.listen: Listen to When You Gonna Learn and notice the lyrics: what are they about, and how does the music fit?

werk/jan-akkerman-eli.text:
Eli is a collaborative album by the Dutch guitarist Jan Akkerman and the vocalist Kaz Lux. It is a concept album with jazz, pop and funk, and thus a departure from the progressive rock of Focus, Akkerman's previous band. Besides them, Jasper van 't Hof and Rick van der Linden play keyboards, Warwick Reading bass and Pierre van der Linden drums. Akkerman also plays bass himself.

In 1976 the record won the Dutch Edison for best album. Strindberg was written as a tribute to the work of August Strindberg. The album has nine tracks, ranging from three to almost six minutes.
werk/jan-akkerman-eli.listen: Listen to Strindberg, the shortest track on the album, and notice how the guitar relates to the keyboards.

werk/jan-akkerman-profile.text:
Profile is an album by the Dutch guitarist Jan Akkerman. It opens with Fresh Air, a piece of almost twenty minutes consisting of seven parts. A series of short tracks follows, from a minute and a half to just over four minutes.

Akkerman plays guitar and bass and is accompanied by the bassist Bert Ruiter and the drummer Pierre van der Linden. On the last track, Stick, the pianist Ferry Maat, the bassist Jaap van Eik and the drummer Frans Smit play along. The choice of repertoire is remarkable: alongside original work there are pieces by Matteo Carcassi and Anton Diabelli, plus the anonymous dance Kemp's Jig. In this way classical guitar music stands beside a long jazz composition.
werk/jan-akkerman-profile.listen: In Fresh Air, listen to how a piece of almost twenty minutes is built from seven parts: notice the moments at which the music changes character.

werk/jan-garbarek-aftenland.text:
Aftenland is an album by the Norwegian saxophonist and composer Jan Garbarek and the organist Kjell Johnsen. They recorded it in December 1979 in the Engelbrekt Church in Stockholm. The album was released the following year on ECM.

It is a duo record with an unusual line-up. Garbarek plays soprano and tenor saxophone and wooden flute, Johnsen plays the church's pipe organ. They wrote all nine pieces together, with titles such as Syn, Linje, Enigma and Iskirken. They are both short and long: Linje lasts less than two minutes, Kilden just over seven. AllMusic gave the album two stars.
werk/jan-garbarek-aftenland.listen: Listen to the title track Aftenland and notice how the saxophone and the pipe organ sound together in the space of the church.

werk/jan-garbarek-dis.text:
The saxophonist Jan Garbarek recorded Dis in December 1976 for the ECM label. The album was released in May 1977. The producer was Manfred Eicher, the recording was done by Jan Erik Kongshaug. Garbarek plays soprano and tenor saxophone and wooden flute. He is accompanied by the American guitarist Ralph Towner on twelve-string and classical guitar. In Skygger the Norwegian brass ensemble Den Norske Messingsekstett joins in. On Vandrere, Viddene and Dis a wind harp can also be heard, an instrument played by the wind itself.

The Penguin Guide to Jazz included Dis in its list of recommended core recordings.
werk/jan-garbarek-dis.listen: Listen to Dis and notice the wind harp. Hear how that soft, wind-played sound blends with the saxophone and the guitar.

werk/jan-garbarek-esoteric-circle.text:
Esoteric Circle is the second album by the Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek. It was originally released under the group name The Esoteric Circle on Flying Dutchman, Bob Thiele's label. Later it was reissued on the Freedom label, this time under his own name. Here he plays with the guitarist Terje Rypdal, the bassist Arild Andersen and the drummer Jon Christensen.

It is a raw, adventurous record. Garbarek plays only tenor saxophone, drawing mainly on the work of Albert Ayler and John Coltrane. His approach is much fiercer and more aggressive than the style for which he later became known on ECM. The nine pieces are all his own, ranging from short sketches of one or two minutes to extended tracks of almost nine minutes. AllMusic gave four stars and found the record comparable to what Tony Williams and John McLaughlin were doing at the time.
werk/jan-garbarek-esoteric-circle.listen: Listen to Traneflight and notice how fierce and direct the tenor saxophone sounds, very different from the restrained sound for which Garbarek later became known.

werk/jan-garbarek-triptykon.text:
Triptykon was recorded on 8 November 1972 and released the following year on ECM. It is the fourth album by the Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek and his third for that label. He plays in a trio with the bassist Arild Andersen and the drummer Edward Vesala, and himself alternates between soprano saxophone, tenor saxophone, bass saxophone and flute.

The music draws on free improvisation and on Scandinavian folk melodies, such as the traditional Bruremarsj. This produces a dark and at times bare sound. AllMusic compared it to a sonic version of Edvard Munch, roaring, stumbling and staggering. Stuart Nicholson of Jazzwise counted the record among the five most important recordings by this saxophonist and spoke of a radical turn in his style.
werk/jan-garbarek-triptykon.listen: Listen to Bruremarsj and notice how a traditional folk melody takes on an expressive sound of its own in this trio.

werk/janet-jackson-all-for-you.text:
All for You is Janet Jackson's seventh studio album, released on 16 April 2001 by Virgin Records. After her divorce from René Elizondo Jr., she wanted to make a lighter record than The Velvet Rope, which was about, among other things, domestic violence and depression. Besides Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, she worked, for the first time since Control, with another producer as well: the hip hop producer Rockwilder.

It is pop and R&B with influences from rock, disco, funk and East Asian music. The songs are about romance, passion and sex, but also about betrayal. China Love uses gamelan and tabla. The title song spent seven weeks at number 1 on the American Hot 100 and won a Grammy for best dance recording. The album was well received, but the explicit lyrics led to bans in some countries.
werk/janet-jackson-all-for-you.listen: Listen to China Love and notice which instruments give it its oriental atmosphere.

werk/janet-jackson-damita-jo.text:
Damita Jo is Janet Jackson's eighth studio album and is named after her middle name. She began it in August 2002, after the All for You Tour, and worked on it until February 2004: eighteen months, the longest recording period of her career. Besides Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis she brought in new producers, including Babyface, Dallas Austin, Kanye West and Scott Storch. The album was released in March 2004, shortly after her Super Bowl performance in which her breast was accidentally exposed.

It is R&B, pop and hip hop about love, romance and lust. In it she plays with alter egos such as Damita Jo and Strawberry, and intimate interludes appear between the tracks. Critics praised the production but found the album too long and too sexual. The record industry blacklisted her singles, which dampened its success.
werk/janet-jackson-damita-jo.listen: Listen to My Baby, in which Kanye West takes part, and notice how his production and her soft voice come together.

werk/janet-jackson-dream-street.text:
Dream Street was released in September 1984 on A&M Records and was Janet Jackson's second album. It sounded more like pop than her debut, which had been more soul. Her father Joe thought the record would be a great success, but it was a disappointment. The album got no further than number 147 on the American chart. The only modest hit was Don't Stand Another Chance, which her brother Marlon produced, with vocal improvisations by Michael Jackson. The track Dream Street received her first music video, filmed during the recording of the TV series Fame.

AllMusic later wrote that the record has the gloss of 1980s pop, with strong synthesizers by John Barnes and Minneapolis funk in Pretty Boy.
werk/janet-jackson-dream-street.listen: Listen to Don't Stand Another Chance and notice the synthesizers in the extended version, in which you can hear the sound of 1984.

werk/janet-jackson-rhythm-nation-1814.text:
Rhythm Nation 1814 is Janet Jackson's fourth studio album and was released on 18 and 19 September 1989 on A&M Records. The record company wanted a follow-up to Control, but she wanted to make a concept album about social problems. With Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis she worked at Flyte Tyme Studios in Minneapolis on tracks about racism, poverty and drug use, alongside love. Her inspiration came from the news, including the shooting at a schoolyard in Stockton. The title names the year in which The Star-Spangled Banner was written.

The sound combines new jack swing, hard rock, pop and industrial influences, with many samples and strongly swinging synthesizer drums. There are mechanical dance rhythms and soft ballads. Miss You Much, Escapade, Black Cat and Love Will Never Do (Without You) went to number one in the United States. It was the best-selling album of 1990 there. Critics see it as her artistic peak.
werk/janet-jackson-rhythm-nation-1814.listen: Listen to Rhythm Nation and notice the heavily swinging, mechanical rhythms beneath the vocals.

werk/janet-jackson-the-velvet-rope.text:
After her first compilation album, in 1995, Janet Jackson renewed her contract with Virgin for eighty million dollars, at the time the biggest record contract ever. During a tour she suffered an emotional breakdown and struggled with depression for a long time. That became the starting point for The Velvet Rope, which she conceived as a concept album about self-examination. She wrote and produced it with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis and with René Elizondo Jr. as co-writer. The title stands for emotional boundaries and the need to feel special.

The lyrics deal with depression, self-worth, domestic violence and sexuality, including homosexuality and BDSM. The music mixes R&B, pop, trip hop, folk, jazz, rock and techno. On Got 'Til It's Gone we hear Q-Tip and a sample of Big Yellow Taxi by Joni Mitchell. The album reached number one on the American chart and Together Again became an international number one. Jackson received a GLAAD Media Award for the album.
werk/janet-jackson-the-velvet-rope.listen: In Got 'Til It's Gone, listen to the sample of Joni Mitchell and the rap by Q-Tip. Notice how those two worlds come together in this track.

werk/janis-joplin-pearl.text:
This album was released in January 1971, three months after the death of Janis Joplin on 4 October 1970. It was her second and last solo album and the only one with the Full Tilt Boogie Band, her last touring band. The producer Paul Rothchild, known from the Doors, called her a producer's dream. At Sunset Sound Recorders in Los Angeles they created a smoother sound than on her earlier records. Many of the songs had already been played on stage in Canada, during the Festival Express train tour.

On Me and Bobby McGee by Kris Kristofferson she plays acoustic guitar herself, and it became a number 1 hit. Trust Me is by Bobby Womack, Get It While You Can by Howard Tate, and she co-wrote Mercedes Benz. Buried Alive in the Blues remained instrumental, because her vocals were not yet on it. Mercedes Benz was the last thing she recorded. The album spent nine weeks at the top of the Billboard 200.
werk/janis-joplin-pearl.listen: Listen to Mercedes Benz, which she sang a cappella. It is the last track she recorded, a few days before her death.

werk/jay-mcshann-the-last-of-the-blue-de.text:
The Last of the Blue Devils is an album by the jazz pianist Jay McShann, recorded in 1977 and released by Atlantic. He plays piano and electric piano and sings, with a small band: Joe Newman on trumpet, Paul Quinichette and Buddy Tate on tenor sax, John Scofield on electric guitar, Milt Hinton on bass and Jackie Williams on drums.

The ten tracks range from blues and swing, such as Confessin' the Blues and Hootie Blues, to Jumpin' at the Woodside by Count Basie and Kansas City. The Globe and Mail wrote that the small line-up is ideal for bringing an old swing number like Jumpin' at the Woodside back to life, and that his singing on 'Tain't Nobody's Bizness If I Do adds a comic touch. AllMusic called the record a whole course in the history of blues-based jazz and strongly recommended it.
werk/jay-mcshann-the-last-of-the-blue-de.listen: Listen to 'Tain't Nobody's Bizness If I Do and notice the singing: the newspaper heard a comic touch in it.

werk/jay-z-in-my-lifetime-vol-1.text:
After the sudden death of The Notorious B.I.G. in March 1997, this was Jay-Z's first album. It was released on 4 November 1997 on Roc-A-Fella Records and Def Jam. A large part of the beats came from The Hitmen, Puff Daddy's production team, which makes the record sound smoother than its predecessor Reasonable Doubt. The mafia themes gave way to the so-called jiggy era of the late 1990s. Guests included Lil' Kim, Foxy Brown, Babyface and Blackstreet.

He himself said that Reasonable Doubt was an introduction and that this album contains more detail and personality. The death of The Notorious B.I.G. influenced The City Is Mine, among others. The record reached number three on the Billboard 200 and went platinum. The reviews were mixed, with praise for his lyrics and criticism of the pop producers.
werk/jay-z-in-my-lifetime-vol-1.listen: In The City Is Mine (feat. Blackstreet), listen to the first verse. According to the rapper himself, the influence of The Notorious B.I.G. can be heard there.

werk/jay-z-reasonable-doubt.text:
For a long time Jay-Z could not get a record deal, even though he had toured with Big Daddy Kane. He sold his tapes from his car, got a deal with Payday Records and left it again. Together with Damon Dash and Kareem Biggs Burke he founded Roc-A-Fella Records, in a cheap office on John Street. He recorded Reasonable Doubt at D&D Studios. The beats came from, among others, DJ Premier, Ski, Knobody and Clark Kent, and the sessions were often a competition. On Brooklyn's Finest, the Notorious B.I.G. raps along, in a friendly duel in which neither of them had written down his lyrics.

The record was released on 25 June 1996. It revolves around mafia themes and raw lyrics about life as a hustler, and according to one writer he also tells what that life does to a person's peace of mind. Critics were positive and many hip hop fans still see this as his best work.
werk/jay-z-reasonable-doubt.listen: Listen to Brooklyn's Finest and notice how the two rappers challenge each other. Who sounds the most sure of themselves?

werk/jay-z-the-dynasty-roc-la-familia.text:
Jay-Z released The Dynasty on 31 October 2000 on Roc-A-Fella Records. The album was first announced as a compilation of artists from the label, such as Memphis Bleek, Beanie Sigel, Amil and Freeway, but was ultimately marketed as a solo album. It is his fifth studio album. The production came mainly from Just Blaze, Kanye West, Bink! and The Neptunes.

The first single was I Just Wanna Love U (Give It 2 Me), made by The Neptunes and incorporating elements of Give It to Me Baby by Rick James. It became one of the rapper's most successful singles. Soon You'll Understand contains a sample of the love theme from the film The Landlord. The album entered at number one on the Billboard 200 and received positive reviews.
werk/jay-z-the-dynasty-roc-la-familia.listen: Listen to I Just Wanna Love U (Give It 2 Me). Notice the beat by The Neptunes and the reference to Rick James.

werk/jay-z-vol-2-hard-knock-life.text:
This third studio album by Jay-Z was released on 29 September 1998 on Roc-A-Fella Records and Def Jam. The rapper wanted to be the voice of people who have no microphone of their own, and in the sleeve notes he himself talked about various tracks. The sound is rougher than on its predecessor In My Lifetime, Vol. 1, mainly because of three tracks by Swizz Beatz. For more pop-oriented work he brought in Timbaland, Jermaine Dupri and Irv Gotti.

The title track builds on a sample from the musical Annie, which the critic Robert Christgau called daring. Christgau also praised the quick way in which the rapper lays down his words. The album went straight in at number 1 on the Billboard 200 and won a Grammy for Best Rap Album, but he boycotted the ceremony because the rap categories were not broadcast. Rolling Stone later placed it at number 46 among the best albums of the 1990s.
werk/jay-z-vol-2-hard-knock-life.listen: Listen to Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem) and notice how a song from a children's musical forms the basis of a hard rap beat.

werk/jean-michel-jarre-equinoxe.text:
Équinoxe was released on 1 December 1978 on Dreyfus, and released worldwide in 1979 by Polydor. Jean-Michel Jarre recorded the album between January and August 1978 in a makeshift studio in his apartment in Paris, on a 16-track recorder. Whereas his previous album Oxygène came about without a concept, he now wanted to sketch a day in a human life, from waking to going to sleep. The sound engineer Michel Geiss built the rain, storm and water animations and designed the Matrisequencer 250, one of the most important instruments on the record. The cover shows the painting Le trac by Michel Granger.

The British press reacted negatively at the time, but later reviews are more favourable. Equinoxe Part 5 reached the British singles chart. On 14 July 1979 Jarre gave a concert on the Place de la Concorde in Paris for more than a million people.
werk/jean-michel-jarre-equinoxe.listen: Listen to the opening piece, THE WATCHERS (movement 1), and notice how the synthesizers and the sound effects together build an atmosphere.

werk/jean-michel-jarre-oxygene.text:
Jean-Michel Jarre worked for years with early synthesizers and tape loops, and came into contact with the musique concrète of Pierre Schaeffer. For this record he built a makeshift studio in the kitchen of his apartment in Paris, with, among other things, an EMS VCS 3 and an ARP 2600. The sound engineer Michel Geiss helped with the purchase and programming of the instruments. The recording ran from August to November 1976. Plenty of echo and reverb was meant to give a great sense of space, and with sounds such as birds and waves the music refers to nature.

The record is entirely instrumental and sounds like symphonic electronic music with bubbling sequences and catchy melodies. Oxygène (Part IV) became a worldwide hit and brought him his breakthrough. The album reached number one in France and number two in England. It is described as the record that led the synthesizer revolution of the 1970s, and later influenced Moby, among others.
werk/jean-michel-jarre-oxygene.listen: Listen to Oxygene, Pt. 14 and notice the echo and the bubbling synthesizer sounds that together evoke a sense of space.

werk/jean-michel-jarre-zoolook.text:
Zoolook was released in November 1984 on Disques Dreyfus. Jean-Michel Jarre drew inspiration from his former teacher Pierre Schaeffer and his musique concrète. He recorded voices and speech in twenty-five languages and, together with Frederick Rousseau, worked on them for three months on the Fairlight CMI, a digital sampler. This approach had already begun on Les Chants Magnétiques and Music for Supermarkets.

Much was recorded in Jarre's own studio in Croissy-sur-Seine. In New York, guest musicians such as Adrian Belew and Marcus Miller played on it. Laurie Anderson sang on Diva in an invented language. The record was more difficult than earlier works and reached only number 47 in the United Kingdom. It did win the Grand Prix du Disque and the prize for best instrumental album at the Victoires de la Musique. Colin Larkin called it a pivotal moment in the history of sampling.
werk/jean-michel-jarre-zoolook.listen: Listen to Diva and notice the voice of Laurie Anderson, who speaks an invented language.

werk/jeff-beck-blow-by-blow.text:
Blow by Blow is the first album released under Jeff Beck's name as a solo artist. It was recorded in October 1974 and released in 1975 on Epic Records. The trio Beck, Bogert & Appice had split up in the spring of 1974, and Beck decided to make a record with instrumental tracks only. He brought back the keyboard player Max Middleton and asked George Martin to produce.

Stevie Wonder contributed two tracks: Cause We've Ended as Lovers and Thelonius, on which he also plays clavinet. There is also a cover of She's a Woman by the Beatles and a piece by Bernie Holland. The other tracks came from Beck and Middleton, and Martin wrote string arrangements for the closing track of each side. The album reached number 4 on the American album chart and is still Beck's most successful album.
werk/jeff-beck-blow-by-blow.listen: Listen to Cause We've Ended as Lovers and notice how the guitar sounds like a singing voice, without a singer.

werk/jeff-beck-flash.text:
Flash is guitarist Jeff Beck's fifth studio album and was released in July 1985 on Epic. It was meant as an excursion into the pop of the time, and Nile Rodgers therefore produced the album. There is singing on almost all the tracks. The guitarist sang himself, at Rodgers's insistence, on Get Workin' and Night After Night, and Rod Stewart came back for People Get Ready. Only Escape and You Know, We Know are instrumental. Escape won a Grammy in 1986 for best rock instrumental performance.

Critics heard dance rock and funk, with many synthesizers and drum machines. The reviews varied. One writer thought it one of his best records, another felt that he played a supporting role on his own album. He himself was later not happy with it.
werk/jeff-beck-flash.listen: Listen to Escape, an instrumental track without vocals. Notice how the guitar takes the place of the voice.

werk/jeff-beck-wired.text:
Wired is the British guitarist Jeff Beck's second solo album and was released in 1976 on Epic Records. Like its predecessor it is an instrumental album, once again with George Martin as producer. Four tracks were written by the drummer Narada Michael Walden and one by the synthesizer player Jan Hammer. Beck also chose Goodbye Pork Pie Hat, Charles Mingus's tribute to the saxophonist Lester Young, and Led Boots had also long been part of his live repertoire.

Hammer plays synthesizer on a number of tracks, Max Middleton plays clavinet and Fender Rhodes. On release the reviews were mostly positive: Rolling Stone called the record full of fire and imagination, although Robert Christgau found it technically accomplished but soulless. Allmusic places Blow by Blow and Wired together as a benchmark for instrumental rock. The record reached number 16 on the American chart.
werk/jeff-beck-wired.listen: Listen to Goodbye Pork Pie Hat and notice how calm and singing the guitar plays here, unlike in the rock pieces on the album.

werk/jeff-lorber-private-passion.text:
Private Passion is the fourth album by the American keyboard player Jeff Lorber and was released in 1986 on Warner Bros. Records. Karyn White and Michael Jeffries, who also played with Tower of Power, sing on the album. The artist himself plays mainly synthesizers and programs many of the parts.

It became his most successful album: it reached number 68 on the Billboard 200. The track Facts of Love reached number 27 on the Billboard Hot 100 and remained his only top-forty hit. The record also launched Karyn White's solo career. He himself was not happy with the direction of his solo albums of that period, in which he felt more like an accompanist in a vocal, R&B-oriented approach. He then took a break until 1993.
werk/jeff-lorber-private-passion.listen: Listen to Facts of Love and notice the position of Karyn White's vocals in relation to the synthesizers.

werk/jeff-lorber-west-side-stories.text:
West Side Stories is the eleventh studio album by Jeff Lorber, a keyboard player and pioneer of smooth jazz. It was released in 1994 on Verve Forecast. He wrote the eleven tracks largely himself, and he also produced and engineered the record himself. Many guests take part, including Paulinho da Costa, Paul Jackson Jr., Michael Landau, Hubert Laws, Art Porter Jr. and Paul Pesco.

Eric Benét sings the lead vocal on Say Love, CeCe Peniston on Don't Forget the Love. Hubert Laws plays flute on No Regrets, and in Tuva the throat singing of Kongar-ol Ondar can be heard. The album reached number five on the American contemporary jazz chart.
werk/jeff-lorber-west-side-stories.listen: Listen to Tuva and notice the throat singing of Kongar-ol Ondar, which gives the track a colour all its own.

werk/jeff-lorber-worth-waiting-for.text:
Worth Waiting For is the tenth studio album by the keyboard player Jeff Lorber. It was released in January 1993 on Verve Forecast and marked his return to his own work after eight years spent making music for others. In that time he produced dance remixes and albums by the saxophonists Dave Koz and Eric Marienthal. He had grown tired of compromise with other artists and wanted to have creative control again himself.

The album continues the line of his 1980s work: smooth jazz and fusion with plenty of synthesizers, blended with R&B, funk and pop. It spent thirty weeks on the Billboard Contemporary Jazz chart, reached number one at the end of July 1993 and sold more than a hundred thousand copies. It is the only album of his to reach number 1 there.
werk/jeff-lorber-worth-waiting-for.listen: Listen to the title track Worth Waiting For and notice the role of the synthesizers in the jazz fusion of this album.

werk/jefferson-airplane-after-bathing-at.text:
After Bathing at Baxter's is the third album by Jefferson Airplane, released on 27 November 1967 by RCA Victor. The band had just come out of the success of Surrealistic Pillow and the single Somebody to Love. After hearing Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, they rejected earlier recordings and opted for more experiment. The recording took five months and cost ten times as much as that of the previous record.

The sound is heavier than on its predecessor, with more fuzz and feedback in Jorma Kaukonen's guitar playing. Rejoyce is jazz-like and refers to Ulysses by James Joyce. Spare Chaynge was cut from a 24-minute recording. Commercially the record was a disappointment: it got no further than number 17 on the Billboard chart. Jann Wenner wrote in Rolling Stone that it was probably the best rock album an American group had made up to that point.
werk/jefferson-airplane-after-bathing-at.listen: Listen to Two Heads and notice how the lyrics drift by like a stream of thoughts.

werk/jefferson-airplane-surrealistic-pil.text:
At the beginning of 1967 the line-up of Jefferson Airplane had just been renewed: the singer Grace Slick joined the band in October 1966, together with the drummer Spencer Dryden. Two weeks later they began their second album at RCA Victor's studio in Hollywood, under the direction of the producer Rick Jarrard. RCA wanted a commercial result, so long psychedelic jams were left out.

The sound has a folk-rock base with psychedelic colours. Slick brought Somebody to Love and White Rabbit with her from her time with The Great Society. White Rabbit became her signature song and is regarded as one of the first openly pro-drug rock songs. Somebody to Love was given a punchier arrangement, and Today is a delicate ballad that was often played on the radio. Somebody to Love and White Rabbit became top-ten hits in the United States and the record is regarded as one of the most important works of early psychedelic rock.
werk/jefferson-airplane-surrealistic-pil.listen: In White Rabbit, listen to the voice of Grace Slick and to how the track, from a quiet start, builds more and more tension.

werk/jerry-goldsmith-the-omen.text:
The Omen is the soundtrack of the 1976 film of the same name, directed by Richard Donner. Jerry Goldsmith was paid 25,000 dollars for the music and at first did not really know what to do. One evening he told his wife Carol that he was hearing voices. That became the starting point: a score with a great deal of choir and an ominous Latin chant, unlike his usual style. The National Philharmonic Orchestra played under the direction of Lionel Newman.

For the theme song Ave Satani, the composer created a kind of satanic Gregorian chant, with reversed Latin phrases from the Mass. Critics praised the score. He won his only Oscar for best original score, after eight earlier nominations. Ave Satani was also nominated for best original song.
werk/jerry-goldsmith-the-omen.listen: Listen to Ave Satani and notice the choir: it sings Latin phrases constructed like a reversed Mass.

werk/jimi-hendrix-both-sides-of-the-sky.text:
This album was released on 9 March 2018 on Legacy Recordings and Experience Hendrix. It is the third and final instalment in a series of releases of archive recordings by Jimi Hendrix, intended as a follow-up to Electric Ladyland. Valleys of Neptune and People, Hell and Angels had appeared earlier. Of the thirteen tracks, ten had never been released before. The recordings come from the Jimi Hendrix Experience and from Band of Gypsys, almost all made at the Record Plant Studios in New York.

Guests play on a few tracks: Stephen Stills, Johnny Winter and Lonnie Youngblood. Sean Westergaard of AllMusic called it surprising how much material even fanatical collectors did not yet know. He picked the instrumental Cherokee Mist, with Hendrix on electric sitar, as the highlight. He found the album a little uneven here and there, but worthwhile for the true fan.
werk/jimi-hendrix-both-sides-of-the-sky.listen: Listen to Cherokee Mist and notice the tone colour of the electric sitar, which takes the place of a singing voice here.

werk/jimi-hendrix-purple-haze.text: In 1966 the American guitarist Jimi Hendrix came to London and formed the Jimi Hendrix Experience there with two British musicians. Purple Haze was released on 17 March 1967. Hendrix used distortion and feedback as a sound, not as a mistake. British guitarists such as Eric Clapton and Jeff Beck came to watch and were impressed. In June 1967 he played at the Monterey Pop Festival and became a star in America too.
werk/jimi-hendrix-purple-haze.listen: The intro begins with a tritone, the interval that was once called the devil's interval. Then comes the Hendrix chord, E7#9.

werk/jimi-hendrix-the-cry-of-love.text:
This was the first album to appear after the death of Jimi Hendrix, on 5 March 1971, half a year after his death. It consists mainly of tracks he recorded in 1970 at his new Electric Lady Studios in New York, with the drummer Mitch Mitchell and the bassist Billy Cox, for a planned fourth studio record. About half were nearly finished. The rest was mixed after his death and sometimes touched up by the engineer Eddie Kramer and Mitchell.

Ten tracks were chosen, including Freedom, Ezy Ryder, Angel and In from the Storm. Straight Ahead and My Friend replaced two tracks that were kept back for a later release. Hendrix had had a double album in mind, but this became a single record. Critics saw it as an impressive tribute. The album reached the charts in both countries and was certified platinum in America in 1998.
werk/jimi-hendrix-the-cry-of-love.listen: Listen to Freedom and notice how Hendrix's guitar comes together with the sharp rhythm of Cox and Mitchell.

werk/jimmy-cliff-the-power-and-the-glory.text:
The Power and the Glory is a 1983 album by the Jamaican musician Jimmy Cliff. He wrote seven of the tracks and was accompanied by his band Oneness. Earl Chinna Smith played guitar, and Kool & the Gang worked on a few tracks. Reggae Night, co-written by La Toya Jackson, was nominated for a Grammy for best reggae recording. Piece of the Pie and American Dream are protest songs. The first quotes lyrics by Bob Marley from Them Belly Full (But We Hungry).

The reviews were mixed. One newspaper found the smooth production and the beautiful tenor not enough to hold the attention. Another praised the light reggae rhythms with familiar R&B melodies. AllMusic heard a hybrid of reggae and pop, far from the raw battle songs of earlier days.
werk/jimmy-cliff-the-power-and-the-glory.listen: Listen to Piece of the Pie and notice the lyrics, which quote a protest song by Bob Marley.

werk/jimmy-eat-world-bleed-american.text:
After the failure of Clarity, Capitol dropped the band in late 1999. The members took on odd jobs, toured through Europe to raise money and paid for the recording with it. In October and November 2000 they recorded the album in Los Angeles, with Mark Trombino as producer. The sound was more direct and accessible than on Clarity, with simpler chords. During the sessions the band put demos on Napster.

After the attacks of 11 September 2001, the album was temporarily released under the name Jimmy Eat World. The Middle, written in response to an email from a fan who felt not punk enough, reached number one on the Modern Rock Tracks chart and number five on the Hot 100. Critics appreciated the record, and several magazines put it on their year-end lists.
werk/jimmy-eat-world-bleed-american.listen: Listen to A Praise Chorus and notice the bridge, in which Davey von Bohlen quotes all kinds of other songs: how many do you recognise?

werk/jimmy-eat-world-clarity.text:
After the commercial failure of Static Prevails in 1996, nobody expected much of Jimmy Eat World any more. The record company Capitol no longer had any interest in the band and thereby left it free. In May and June 1998 the band recorded the album with the producer Mark Trombino, first the drums at Sound City in Van Nuys, then forty days for guitars and overdubs at Clear Lake Audio in North Hollywood. On this album Jim Adkins took over the lead vocals from Tom Linton.

The sound is described as emo, pop punk and punk rock, with cello, piano, violins, bells and two drum kits on tracks such as Lucky Denver Mint, Ten and Goodbye Sky Harbor. Critics praised the dynamics. Even so, success failed to come and Capitol dropped the band in August 1999. Only later did Clarity grow into a cult classic, and Kerrang!, LA Weekly and Rolling Stone in particular regard it as one of the best emo albums ever.
werk/jimmy-eat-world-clarity.listen: Listen to Table for Glasses and notice the cello. The band learned here that few instruments can create great dynamics, if you bring them in at the right moment.

werk/jimmy-eat-world-static-prevails.text:
Static Prevails is the second studio album by the American band Jimmy Eat World and was released on 23 July 1996 on Capitol Records. After their 1994 debut, the band signed to the label in 1995, partly thanks to a split single with Christie Front Drive. The bassist Mitchel Porter had left to become a missionary, and Rick Burch took his place. The recording took place at Sound City in Los Angeles and Big Fish in Encinitas, with Wes Kidd, Mark Trombino and the band as producers.

The group left skate punk and pop punk behind and chose a more aggressive sound, somewhere between post-hardcore, emo and punk. Digits was the first track in that new style. Call It in the Air was the first single and Rockstar received a music video. The reviews were mixed, but the record is now regarded as a benchmark for the second wave of emo.
werk/jimmy-eat-world-static-prevails.listen: Listen to Digits and notice how the track departs from the earlier pop punk, with a rawer and more intense sound.

werk/jimmy-giuffre-tangents-in-jazz.text:
Tangents in Jazz is Jimmy Giuffre's second album and was released on Capitol. The recording took place in June 1955 at Capitol Studios in Los Angeles, in three sessions. Giuffre played clarinet, tenor saxophone and baritone saxophone. He was accompanied by the trumpeter Jack Sheldon, the bassist Ralph Peña and the drummer Artie Anton. There is no piano, which keeps the sound open and light.

Giuffre wrote nine of the ten tracks himself. Only This Is My Beloved is by Vernon Duke. Four short pieces are called Scintilla and run like a thread through the record. According to AllMusic's overview, the emphasis is on a Cool Jazz tone and relaxed improvisation, with hints of folk music, but sounding very modern for its time.
werk/jimmy-giuffre-tangents-in-jazz.listen: In Scintilla I, the shortest track, listen to the relaxed, light tone of the horns, and then compare that with Scintilla II.

werk/jimmy-giuffre-western-suite.text:
Western Suite was released in 1960 on the Atlantic label. The composer and arranger Jimmy Giuffre chose an unusual trio of clarinet, guitar and valve trombone, with Jim Hall and Bob Brookmeyer, without a rhythm section. The first half is a four-part suite inspired by country and folk. The second half consists of a long, abstract version of the big band standard Topsy and a piece by Thelonious Monk, Blue Monk.

Thom Jurek of Allmusic wrote that the score is set up so that every player has to stand on their own feet, with no comfort zone. According to him it swings like West Coast jazz, but is as ambitious as Copland's Billy the Kid. In DownBeat in 1961, Ira Gitler called the interplay of the three remarkable and found lyricism and depth of feeling in it.
werk/jimmy-giuffre-western-suite.listen: Listen to 1st Movement - Pony Express and follow the guitar and the valve trombone, with no bass or drums beneath them.

werk/jimmy-jam-en-terry-lewis-control.text:
For years Janet Jackson was under the management of her father Joseph, who guided her first two albums. She then had her marriage to James DeBarge annulled, parted ways with her father as manager and chose John McClain of A&M. He introduced her to the production duo Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. Their collaboration produced a new sound, a blend of rhythm and blues, rap, funk, disco and synthetic percussion, with a striking triplet swing that would later inspire new jack swing. The lyrics are about her own life and about becoming independent.

Control was released in February 1986 and was her breakthrough. It became her first number one on the American album chart. Five singles reached the American top five, including What Have You Done for Me Lately, Nasty and When I Think of You, her first number one. Critics praised the album as an artistic achievement and as a personal statement. It was nominated for a Grammy for Album of the Year.
werk/jimmy-jam-en-terry-lewis-control.listen: In Control, listen to the rhythm and the synthetic percussion. Notice how the lyrics express her new independence.

werk/jimmy-smith-home-cookin.text:
Home Cookin’ contains recordings from 1958 and 1959 and was released on Blue Note. Jimmy Smith plays organ, with Kenny Burrell on guitar, Donald Bailey on drums and, on a number of tracks, Percy France on tenor saxophone. Alfred Lion was the producer and Rudy Van Gelder the engineer. The programme consists of pieces by Smith himself and of covers of existing songs: See See Rider by Ma Rainey, I Got a Woman by Ray Charles, and Sugar Hill and Come on Baby by Burrell. On the CD reissue, five bonus tracks were added.

The AllMusic reviewer calls it a recommended starting point for anyone not yet familiar with Smith's music and a substantial addition for connoisseurs. According to The Penguin Guide to Jazz the album is fairly formulaic, but Burrell's presence makes it a solid record.
werk/jimmy-smith-home-cookin.listen: In See See Rider, listen to the interplay of organ, tenor saxophone and guitar.

werk/jimmy-smith-house-party.text:
House Party is the tenth studio album by the organist Jimmy Smith, recorded on 25 August 1957 and 25 February 1958 and released in 1958 on Blue Note. It was his fourteenth release for that label. In those years Blue Note used the Manhattan Towers Hotel Ballroom in New York for larger groups or when New York was more practical for the musicians. The engineer Rudy Van Gelder was still working in his parents' house in Hackensack at that time. House Party was the first of two Smith albums recorded on two different dates; the second was The Sermon!.

Those playing on the sessions included Lee Morgan on trumpet, Curtis Fuller on trombone, Lou Donaldson, Tina Brooks and George Coleman on saxophone, Kenny Burrell on guitar and Art Blakey on drums. An AllMusic reviewer felt that the real pleasure lies in hearing the music itself.
werk/jimmy-smith-house-party.listen: In Lover Man, listen to how small the line-up is: no trumpet and no tenor saxophone play here.

werk/joan-baez-any-day-now.text:
In September 1968 Joan Baez went to Nashville for a marathon session. Two albums came out of it: Any Day Now and, a year later, David's Album. The ninth studio album is a double LP with only songs by Bob Dylan. Baez laid Dylan's sheet music out on the floor, closed her eyes and chose blind; that is how the track list came about. Six songs were at that time not yet on an official Dylan album. Love Is Just a Four-Letter Word he apparently never recorded himself. Baez also drew illustrations for each track, which are printed in the sleeve.

The album reached number 30 on the Billboard chart and was certified gold in 1969. Thom Jurek of AllMusic called her the best interpreter of Dylan and wrote that her voice extends the meaning of the songs.
werk/joan-baez-any-day-now.listen: Listen to Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands and notice how Baez sings Dylan's song in her own voice. Compare how she tells the story with what you know from Dylan.

werk/joan-baez-farewell-angelina.text:
Farewell, Angelina is Joan Baez's fifth studio album and was released in late 1965. It reached number ten on the Billboard Pop Albums chart. For the first time there is electric accompaniment on a record by the singer, in the form of Bruce Langhorne's electric guitar. Others playing include Russ Savakus on bass and Ralph Rinzler on mandolin.

The title comes from a song by Bob Dylan, which is also the opening track here. There are four Dylan songs on it, two of which were not officially released by him until 1991. There is also work by Woody Guthrie and Pete Seeger, including a German version of Where Have All the Flowers Gone. The cover photograph is by Richard Avedon. AllMusic saw the album as part of the growth of folk rock in the 1960s.
werk/joan-baez-farewell-angelina.listen: Listen to It's All Over Now, Baby Blue and notice how the electric guitar accompanies the voice.

werk/joan-baez-noel.text:
Noël is Joan Baez's sixth studio album and her first Christmas album. It was released in November 1966. Together with the arranger and conductor Peter Schickele, known as PDQ Bach, she recorded, for the first time, a record outside the usual folk format with guitar. She also made her next two albums with him, with classical orchestration.

In contrast to many other Christmas albums, she chose mainly traditional material and a serious, restrained tone, not light-hearted or commercial songs. There are well-known titles on it, such as The Little Drummer Boy, and less familiar ones, such as Down in Yon Forest. Schickele also arranged a few short instrumental pieces. The album is dedicated to Pablo Casals, at least The Carol of the Birds is.
werk/joan-baez-noel.listen: Listen to Coventry Carol and notice how sober and restrained it sounds, without any cheerful Christmas atmosphere.

werk/joao-gilberto-amoroso.text:
Amoroso is a 1977 album by João Gilberto on which Brazilian bossa nova is given an orchestral treatment. Gilberto sings and plays guitar, accompanied by a string orchestra written and conducted by the German arranger Claus Ogerman. Tommy LiPuma and Helen Keane produced, Al Schmitt handled recording and mixing. For the album he received a Grammy nomination for best jazz vocal performance.

Most of it is in Portuguese, but for the first time he also sings in English, in the Gershwin song 'S Wonderful. That was new, because he did not speak the language and had long dreaded it. He also sings in Italian in Estate and in Spanish in Bésame Mucho. Four tracks are by Antônio Carlos Jobim and arranged by Gilberto. In 1993 the album was released on CD together with Brasil from 1981.
werk/joao-gilberto-amoroso.listen: Listen to 'S Wonderful and notice how his soft guitar and voice relate to Ogerman's strings.

werk/joao-gilberto-chega-de-saudade.text:
Chega de Saudade was the debut album of the Brazilian singer and guitarist João Gilberto. Many people call it the first bossa nova record. The title means roughly enough of longing, although the word saudade has a richer meaning in Portuguese. When it was released, a newspaper wrote that Gilberto was one of the most musical singers in Brazil, and that his lack of volume was more than made up for by this. The paper praised his taste in the choice of melodies and the sobriety of his singing, for example in Desafinado.

The record continues to receive much praise in the twenty-first century. In 2001 it entered the Grammy Hall of Fame and the Latin Grammy Hall of Fame. In 2002 Brazilian experts placed it third among the best Brazilian records.
werk/joao-gilberto-chega-de-saudade.listen: Listen to Desafinado and notice how soft and restrained Gilberto sings, without ever raising his voice.

werk/joao-gilberto-o-amor-o-sorriso-e-a-.text:
João Gilberto released this album in 1960 in Brazil on the Odeon label, with Aloysio de Oliveira as producer. The title means love, the smile and the flower and comes from the original lyrics of Meditação, a song by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Newton Mendonça. Almost simultaneously the record appeared in the United States under the title Brazil's Brilliant João Gilberto.

AllMusic calls the record of great importance, because it introduced Gilberto, Jobim and with them bossa nova to the American public in 1961, a year before Stan Getz had a hit with Desafinado. Several songs by Jobim, such as One Note Samba, Corcovado and Outra Vez, were heard here in North America for the first time.
werk/joao-gilberto-o-amor-o-sorriso-e-a-.listen: Listen to Corcovado, one of the songs by Jobim that were first heard in North America on this record, and notice the restrained way of singing.

werk/joe-cocker-jamaica-say-you-will.text:
Jamaica Say You Will was released in April 1975 as Joe Cocker's fifth studio album. The tracks come from the same sessions as I Can Stand a Little Rain from 1974, the record that received much praise. The album did less well than its predecessor. Jim Price produced it at The Village Recorder in Los Angeles, and the rhythm section is mostly the Kingpins, formerly the backing band of the saxophonist King Curtis, with Bernard Purdie on drums.

Randy Newman plays a part: he wrote I Think It's Going to Rain Today and Lucinda. The sound is mainly soul and blues. In (That's What I Like) In My Woman, a fast rhythm section with horns can be heard. Where Am I Now and I Think It's Going to Rain Today run into one another and mirror each other's feeling. Oh Mama is pure blues vocal with saxophone, and the album ends acoustically with Jack-a-Diamonds, a simple, folk-like track.
werk/joe-cocker-jamaica-say-you-will.listen: Listen to Oh Mama and notice how Cocker's voice, with only a saxophone for company, carries the track.

werk/joe-cocker-joe-cocker.text:
Joe Cocker! is his second studio album, released in November 1969. As on the first LP, it consists mainly of covers: Dear Landlord comes from Bob Dylan, Bird on the Wire from Leonard Cohen, She Came In Through the Bathroom Window and Something from the Beatles, and Delta Lady and Hello Little Friend from Leon Russell. One track, That's Your Business Now, he wrote together with Chris Stainton. Denny Cordell and Leon Russell produced the record in Hollywood, at A&M Studios and Sunset Sound.

The Grease Band played on it, the group that had also backed him at Woodstock in August 1969. After this album he parted ways with the band, because he did not want to tour, and formed Mad Dogs and Englishmen with Russell. The album reached number 11 on the Billboard 200 in America, and Delta Lady reached number 10 in England.
werk/joe-cocker-joe-cocker.listen: Listen to Delta Lady, a song by Leon Russell, and notice how the singer makes someone else's song his own.
